correctness.rationale: The nonnegative integrated removals are bounded by initial susceptible plus infectious mass, so bounded beta/mu implies finite integrated force. The stable infectious equation with integrable incidence gives I(t,x) tending to zero. Integrating then yields H=B+T(1-exp(-H)), and the surviving mass is m+(S-m)exp(-H). Convexity, the negative value at zero when B>0 and the positive asymptotic slope give one positive root; at that root T exp(-H)=(H-B)/(exp(H)-1)<1. Thus at fixed m<S minimizing remaining weighted exposure strictly improves the objective and the threshold exchange integral gives all equality cases, with arbitrary allocation on the cut level. Adding a positive feasible increment strictly increases survival, so the budget is saturated, including the endpoints. The rearrangement and implicit differentiation give the frontier and its positive marginal term, regular through T=1. The inherited dynamic-control conclusion is about a supremum, not attainment; at the full endpoint it also follows by taking lower budgets tending to S and using S as an upper bound. Independent bounded bisection reproduced the reported two-group survivor masses 1.853622849292 and 1.574692330951. This is corroboration only; the continuum claim rests on the proof and the dynamic equivalence on the cited theorem. Uploaded code was inspected, not run.

value.rationale: The extension resolves a specific open regime in the cited model: finite-seed survivor optimization at budgets that can drive post-vaccination exposure through one. It provides a constructive exact allocation and continuous scalar frontier rather than a simulation, and clarifies why the marginal benefit has no singularity there. The common-hazard, perfect-vaccine objective bounds its practical interpretation.
